newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada seizes three U.S. boats in salmon feud. [CORRECTED 17:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Canada seizes three U.S. boats in salmon feud. [CORRECTED 17:35 GMT]

text.p: Canada has seized three U.S. fishing boats in an escalation of its dispute with Washington over Pacific salmon fishing, officials said on Monday.

Following last week's decision by Canada to strictly enforce regulations on ships passing through its waters after a breakdown in salmon talks, two U.S. trawlers were seized on Sunday and another on Monday. (Corrects days of seizures)

The arrest of the American skippers, who will appear in a British Colombia court on Tuesday, was a clear signal of Ottawa's frustration with the U.S. government and aimed at pressuring Washington to agree to a settlement.

Talks between Canada and the United States on how to share dwindling salmon stocks in the Pacific Northwest collapsed last Tuesday in Seattle. The two neighbours have squabbled for years over salmon catches and pressure for a deal is mounting before this year's salmon run begins in the next few weeks.
British Columbia Premier Glen Clark on Friday accused Ottawa of not pressing hard enough and the United States of not giving its top negotiator authority to make a deal.

The two governments agreed late on Friday to resume negotiations later this week after Clark announced his province was cancelling the lease on an underwater military test range used by the United States.

Ottawa began on Wednesday enforcing an existing regulation that requires all U.S. fishing boats passing through its waters on their way to fishing grounds to report to Canadian authorities and stow their fishing gear.
The three trawlers stopped off the British Columbia coast were escorted to Port Hardy on the northern end of Vancouver Island, Canadian Department of Fisheries official Bud Graham said.
"We have stepped up our enforcement to signal to the United States our displeasure at the failure to reach a salmon treaty," Clark told a local radio station.
Skippers of the three boats face a maximum fine of $500,000 Canadian ($370,000 U.S.) although Graham doubted the maximum penalty would be imposed.
He defended Canada's action, saying the regulations were well known and that the United States had similar rules. "They were fully aware of these requirements...and they failed (to comply)," he said.
